proof:
# Three double core sectors enclose a triangle, and one remaining corner compresses exactly

These are ordinary planar statements for three fixed balanced normals. The first uses a strict half-cap ceiling to prove boundedness of an actual support triangle. The second is an exact geometric replacement, with no smallness or near-triangle assumption. Neither statement changes or controls neighboring mixed fibers.

## 1. Setup and supporting bridge lines

Take normals (1,0),(0,1),(-1,-1), source zero, and a convex body K with zero in its interior. Its cyclic ray endpoints are

    P_0=(A,0), P_1=(0,B), P_2=(-t,t),
    P_3=(-a,0), P_4=(0,-b), P_5=(r,-r),

with all radii positive. Write the three unique-sector areas as X_1,X_2,X_3 in sectors 5,1,3, and the three double-sector areas as Y_1,Y_2,Y_3 in sectors 2,4,0. Assume all three double sectors are their core triangles:

    Y_1=at/2,       Y_2=br/2,       Y_3=AB/2.              (1)

The lines through these three bridge segments support the whole body. Here is why area equality suffices. The intersection of K with a closed sector is convex and contains its core triangle. A proper enlargement of that full-dimensional triangle has positive area, so equality of areas makes the entire sector intersection exactly the core triangle. If a point of K were beyond the line of its outer bridge edge, its segment to a relative-interior point of the bridge would, sufficiently close to that bridge, lie inside the sector and beyond the bridge line, a contradiction.

Consequently K is contained in the intersection D of the three actual bridge halfplanes:

    x/A+y/B <=1,
    x+(1-a/t)y >=-a,
    y+(1-b/r)x >=-b.                                   (2)

The origin is strictly inside all three halfplanes. Each bridge line contains an actual positive-length boundary segment.

Let q_1,q_2,q_3 be the cap areas for x>=0, y>=0, x+y<=0, and let k=|K|. The exact sector identities imply

    q_j+q_l=k-X_i+Y_i       ({i,j,l}={1,2,3}).           (3)

Thus if every q_i<k/2, then X_i>Y_i for every i.

**Support-triangle theorem.** Under (1), if all three q_i<k/2, the set D in (2) is bounded and is a full-dimensional triangle containing K. Its six ray intersections remain the prescribed P_i.

## 2. An unbounded intersection would open through a unique sector

Suppose D were unbounded. Choose points tending to infinity, normalize their directions, and pass to a unit-vector limit e. Dividing each inequality in (2) by the diverging norms shows that e is a nonzero recession direction for all three halfplanes.

Such a direction cannot belong to any closed double-sector cone. The linear functional defining its own bridge halfplane is positive on each nonzero point of that cone: it has value one at both generating ray endpoints, and a point in the cone is a nonnegative linear combination of them. A recession direction would have that functional at most zero. The six cutting rays are also contained in these closed double cones. Therefore e lies in the interior of one unique-sector cone.

Cyclically permute the three normals so that this is unique sector 1. Then e=(s,-u) with s>u>0. Set

    alpha=B/A>0,     beta=b/r>0.

The first and third recession inequalities in (2) imply

    alpha <= u/s <=1-beta,

and hence

    alpha+beta<=1.                                    (4)

In particular 0<alpha,beta<1. We shall show that (4) contradicts X_2>Y_2 and X_3>Y_3 from (3).

## 3. The two finite neighboring-sector envelopes

Put ell=a/t>0 and

    D_2=1-alpha+alpha ell>0,
    D_3=beta+(1-beta)ell>0.

The core halfplanes that bound unique sector 2 give the exact envelope area

    E_2=[2Ba+B^2(1-ell)-at(1-alpha)]/(2D_2),             (5)

and those bounding unique sector 3 give

    E_3=[2ab-b^2(1-ell)-a^2(1-beta)]/(2D_3).            (6)

We justify these formulas and boundary cases explicitly. In sector 2 use nonnegative coordinates

    (x,y)=u P_1+v P_2=(-vt,uB+vt).

The first two bridge halfplanes become

    u+m v<=1,       v-n u<=1,
    m=t(1-alpha)/B>0,       n=B(1-ell)/a.

They contain the two actual ray endpoints, so m<=1 and n>=-1. Their determinant 1+mn=D_2/ell is positive. Their intersection in the nonnegative quadrant is the quadrilateral with coordinate vertices

    (0,0), (1,0), ((1-m)/(1+mn),(1+n)/(1+mn)), (0,1),

allowing coincident consecutive vertices at the boundary values m=1 or n=-1. Since the coordinate Jacobian is Bt, its area is Bt(2+n-m)/[2(1+mn)], which simplifies exactly to (5). K's unique sector is contained in this envelope; the unused third bridge halfplane can only reduce it. Hence X_2<=E_2.

In sector 3 use (x,y)=u P_3+v P_4=(-ua,-vb). The last two bridge halfplanes become

    u+s v<=1,       v+w u<=1,
    s=(1-ell)b/a,       w=(1-beta)a/b>0.

Core containment gives s<=1 and w<=1; also 1-sw=D_3>0. The same quadrant calculation, now with Jacobian ab, gives area ab(2-s-w)/[2(1-sw)], which is (6). Again the formula includes a collapsed additional vertex when one endpoint inequality is an equality, and X_3<=E_3.

## 4. A nonnegative-square contradiction

By (3) and (1), all caps below half would require

    E_2>=X_2>br/2=b^2/(2beta),
    E_3>=X_3>AB/2=B^2/(2alpha).

Multiply the first strict inequality by 2beta D_2, the second by 2alpha D_3, and add. Substituting (5)--(6) and collecting B^2 and b^2 gives

    2a(beta B+alpha b)
       > ell B^2+b^2+beta at(1-alpha)+alpha a^2(1-beta).

Divide by a>0 and use ell/a=1/t. After completing two squares this is exactly

    0 > (B-beta t)^2/t + (b-alpha a)^2/a
                       +(1-alpha-beta)(beta t+alpha a). (7)

Every term on the right is nonnegative by (4). This contradiction proves that D is bounded.

Since D is a bounded intersection of three distinct halfplanes with zero in its interior, it is a triangle. None of the halfplanes is redundant: each boundary contains its actual positive-length bridge segment, and the three lines are distinct. Along every cutting ray, one of these bridge inequalities already has equality at the prescribed endpoint P_i and excludes all farther points on that ray. Since D contains K, its ray endpoints are exactly P_i. This proves the support-triangle theorem.

## 5. An exact one-corner compression, at arbitrary scale

Here is a separate elementary replacement lemma.

Let T be a triangle with source zero and three cuts strictly isolating its three distinct vertices. Let C be the convex hull of its six cutting-ray endpoints. As usual T\C is, up to boundaries, the disjoint union of three corner triangles U_i, each wholly in its vertex's unique sector.

Suppose C subset K subset T and K contains the other two vertices of T, so T\K is contained in just one corner triangle U=conv(V,P,Q). Put

    E=|T|-|K|,       L=|U|>0,

so 0<=E<=L. If E=0 take K'=T. Otherwise set s=sqrt(E/L) in (0,1], define

    P_s=V+s(P-V),        Q_s=V+s(Q-V),

and cut T by the closed halfplane through P_s,Q_s that contains C. The removed corner is precisely conv(V,P_s,Q_s), of area s^2 L=E. Call the retained body K'. It is a quadrilateral, including when s=1 because P,Q lie in the relative interiors of different triangle edges.

The removed corner lies in U, so K' has exactly the same lost volume E in the same unique sector as K, and none in the other sectors. It contains C and is contained in T. Thus its six ray endpoints, all three full central chord sections, all six sector areas, and all three cap areas agree EXACTLY with K. In particular every generalized Lorentz row agrees. No first variation, limiting argument, or small-corner condition is used.

## 6. Application to the (2S,2S,2D) row-maximizing pentagon

Consider the fixed-sector row-maximization reduction and its pentagon graph consisting of two singular two-node blocks and one positive-definite two-node block. Its three positive edges are alternate edges of the six-cycle. If they were all double sectors, every unique sector would be its core triangle. This is incompatible with all caps below half: (3) would give X_i>Y_i for all i, whereas the product of the three unique core areas equals the product of the three opposite double core areas and Y_i is at least its own core area. Multiplying gives a contradiction.

Therefore, in the cap band, the three positive edges are the three UNIQUE sectors, and the three double sectors are cores. The support-triangle theorem gives an actual containing triangle T with the same six endpoints. Every unique sector has positive excess, so each corresponding vertex of T lies strictly in that unique sector. Thus the three cuts strictly isolate its vertices.

The two singular unique-sector blocks force their corner vertices to be exactly the intersections of their adjacent bridge support lines. Indeed their node slacks vanish, so both prescribed endpoints are straight joins; the inserted sector vertex lies on both adjacent bridge lines, whose intersection is the corresponding vertex of T. The exact sector area is therefore the full sector area of T. Since the actual sector of K is a compact convex subset of that full-dimensional sector of T with the same area, the two sectors are equal: proper inclusion would leave positive area. Consequently K itself contains both of these vertices. This conclusion does not assume that a generic auxiliary vertex of a sector replacement belongs to the original body. The remaining positive-definite block is the only possible missing corner.

The body contains the six-ray hull C and lies in T, and differs from T only inside that last unique corner. Section 5 replaces it by a quadrilateral with exactly the same sectors, chords, cap areas and rows. This applies in particular to the maximizing polygon selected by the finite-data reduction. It makes no assertion of uniqueness of the original pentagon.

**Consequence.** Within the strict half-cap band, the (2S,2S,2D) pentagon branch needs no separate row inequality: any putative row violation in it has an exact quadrilateral replacement. The other pentagon block patterns are unaffected by this argument. No mixed-fiber compatibility is preserved or inferred.
